answer.summary: Kaba recommends diagnosing change problems with the five-part “managing complex change” framework—vision, skills, incentives, resources, and an action plan—then targeting the missing element rather than applying a generic fix. 〔S1, S2, S3〕

sections.heading: Diagnose what is missing
sections.content: Check whether the team has a clear vision, the skills to carry out the change, incentives aligned with the desired work, resources in the right places, and a clear action plan. Kaba advises leaders to observe what is happening, including anecdotal challenges, and work out where they can contribute. Missing components can show up in different ways: no vision can produce confusion, misaligned incentives can produce resistance, and no action plan can lead to false starts. The exchange also identifies a skills gap with anxiety; Kaba agrees and advises finding the missing levers within the relevant area. 〔S1, S2, S3〕

sections.heading: Address the specific gap
sections.content: Once you identify the likely gap, determine which levers are missing and focus your effort there. Kaba notes that action plans are easier to institute than some other parts of the framework. As an example of building skills and shared understanding, he describes creating a deck explaining his view of product craft and other topics, giving the team shared language and a repository of skills to build. 〔S2, S3〕

judgment.explanation: The answer accurately presents the five-part managing-complex-change framework, recommends observing the team to identify missing elements and choosing levers to address them, and notes that action plans are easier to institute than other parts of the framework. Its claims are supported by S1–S3.
